content.intro: This lesson covers comparing generative architectures through 6 syllabus subtopics preserved from the supplied Generative AI curriculum. Compare autoregressive, latent-variable, adversarial, diffusion, and other generative approaches by objective, output modality, control, cost, and limitations.
content.why_it_matters: Autoregressive models versus diffusion models is part of the representation and generation mechanism. Follow the information flow from input representation to model computation to output selection, then distinguish the architecture's capabilities from limits caused by data, context, decoding choices, or compute.

items.text: Use likelihood estimation versus sample quality to turn a vague quality claim into an observable criterion. Define a representative dataset, an expected outcome or rubric, a baseline, and the failure categories you will record; interpret aggregate scores alongside examples and affected groups.

items.text: For training costs and inference latency, distinguish the training objective from the evaluation goal. Check provenance and data quality, keep validation/test examples isolated from training, record the baseline and configuration, and evaluate both improvement on the target task and possible regressions elsewhere.

content.task: Practice autoregressive models versus diffusion models within comparing generative architectures: use a small synthetic input, predict the result, run the example, then change one input to test an edge case. Record the expected result and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example uses a clearly described, non-sensitive input.
Expected behavior and at least one edge/failure case are written down.
The learner checks the result against an explicit criterion and records limitations.
hints: Begin with a tiny input whose expected behavior you can explain before running it.
Change one variable at a time and retain a fixed baseline for comparison.
When a model or external service is involved, inspect evidence and errors; do not treat the model response as a trusted instruction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent or plausible output is necessarily correct.
common_mistakes.fix: Use evidence, schema checks, representative test cases, and human review for consequential results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing several inputs or parameters at once.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a baseline and vary one factor at a time so the effect can be interpreted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting secrets or private source material in prompts, logs, or a public example.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic data, server-side secret storage, data minimization, and reviewed retention rules.
